candidates.title: Do learned image captioning metrics generalize? Auditing duplicated samples in human-judgment benchmarks
candidates.content: Learned image captioning metrics are trained and tested on human judgments, so their reported correlation is a claim about generalization. We audit this claim for the three most recent collections of such judgments, Polaris, Nebula, and Spica, matching images at the pixel level. First, test samples reappear in training sets: the Spica training set contains about two-thirds of the Polaris test set, with identical human ratings. Second, controlled retraining shows that duplicates can inflate a metric: for Pearl, the gain is confined to the duplicated samples and grows with every epoch; for DENEB, it stays below one point. The gain depends on the learner and on how often a training set repeats a sample. Third, Kendall's τ over all samples is the sum of two terms, detecting captions with the lowest human score and ranking the others; the first supplies most of the reported correlation and is nearly saturated. The recent test sets cannot order Polos, DENEB and Pearl consistently, and a ridge regression on frozen features matches or exceeds all three. candidates.title: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games?
candidates.content: Games, especially modern AAA games, challenge language models to perceive complex scenes, control actions, and make decisions over long horizons. Existing game benchmarks primarily test language models as computer-use agents that query a language model throughout play, incurring repeated inference cost and, in real-time games, acting while the environment continues to evolve. We ask whether coding agents can learn from game interaction to develop standalone game-playing programs that run without language model inference. We thus introduce Coding4Games, a benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can develop standalone programs that play modern games through visual observations and standard game inputs. candidates.title: LoopDVR: Looped Transformer for Efficient Dense Visual Recognition
candidates.content: We propose LoopDVR, a framework for converting pretrained Transformer-based dense visual recognition models into parameter-efficient looped networks. Rather than reducing the network width or depth directly, LoopDVR reuses Transformer blocks across layers in both the ViT backbone and Transformer decoder, reducing the number of parameters while retaining the original computational structure. However, naively sharing parameters can disrupt the distinct transformations learned at different depths. To address this challenge, we identify suitable sharing groups based on inter-layer representation dissimilarity and keep the final backbone block independent for multi-scale feature construction. We then initialize each shared backbone block with the pretrained weights of its group's terminal layer to better preserve the learned representations. An independent Loop Adapter at each layer further helps retain depth-specific transformations within shared blocks. Subsequently, we distill visual representations into the looped backbone and integrate it with a looped decoder for task-specific training. candidates.title: Rituximab Maintenance in Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis
candidates.content: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is the rarest of the antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)–associated vasculitides and is defined clinically by asthma, eosinophilia, chronic rhinosinusitis, pulmonary infiltrates, and necrotizing vasculitis and eosinophil-rich granulomatous inflammation involving a variety of organ systems. Only 30% to 40% of patients are ANCA positive (usually against myeloperoxidase), and ANCA status often correlates with distinct but overlapping clinical patterns. Historically, glucocorticoids have been the mainstay of EGPA treatment; although the treatment has never been tested adequately prospectively, patients with organ- or life-threatening disease typically receive remission induction with high-dose glucocorticoids plus cyclophosphamide or, in select cases, rituximab. Patients without organ-threatening manifestations have been treated with glucocorticoids alone or in combination with steroid-sparing agents such as azathioprine, methotrexate, or mycophenolate. candidates.title: New Drug Technologies and Their Histories
candidates.content: Here’s a look at how long it can take for new drug technologies to actually make it to the clinic and to FDA approval - including why it takes as long as it does and how that might be sped up. Four techniques get a close look and comparison: fragment-based drug discovery (FBDD), DNA-encoded libraries DEL), aptamers, and targeted protein degradation. I have written posts about all of these over the years (and personally done work on some of them as well!) It’s interesting to note the timelines. For fragments, the first big demonstration was in 1996 and 15 years later the first drug discovered through fragment-based techniques was approved by the FDA. For DEL, the original proof-of-concept was probably around 2004, but to date (as far as this paper’s author has been able to find out) no drugs have been approved that came up by this route, which I hadn’t realized (this could change fairly soon, it should be noted). As for aptamers, their POC came back in 1992 and the first FDA approval in 2004, although there have been only two drugs that have made it that far in over thirty years. candidates.title: Chemotherapy Actually Helps Immunotherapy in Cancer
candidates.content: This paper’s conclusions seem well worth knowing: the authors are looking at the intersection of what are usually considered two rather different forms of cancer treatment (therapeutic vaccines to mobilize the immune system and the more classic chemotherapy approaches). The paper notes that tests of such vaccines often take place in patients who are themselves receiving chemotherapy, and in fact some beneficial interactions have been seen. So they tested some viral-vector vaccines in combination with common chemotherapy (carboplatin plus paclitaxel, “CarboTaxol”) in mice. The added chemotherapy was definitely beneficial compared to the therapeutic vaccine. Previous studies had shown myeloid depletion with the chemotherapy which seemed to aid later vaccine performance, but in this case they were given simultaneously. A close look at the T cells and myeloid cells here suggests that myeloid depletion is indeed part of the story, but not all of it - there are other mechanisms at work that need to be figured out. candidates.content: by Dante G. Calise, Madeline L. Michaelis, Jin Woo Bok, Zhili Chen, Joshua J. Coon, Anna Huttenlocher, Benjamin J. Chadwick, Nancy P. Keller Aspergillus fumigatus is a major opportunistic fungal pathogen whose ability to maintain hyphal integrity and withstand host defenses is critical for virulence. Septal pores, which connect hyphal compartments, are dynamically regulated to preserve cellular integrity under stress, yet the molecular components governing this process remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify and characterize a septal pore-associated protein, SppA, and demonstrate its essential role in maintaining septal integrity in A. fumigatus . Deletion of sppA resulted in defective septal organization and increased susceptibility to hyphal damage. candidates.title: RNA fine-tunes KAT5 activity to shape chromatin acetylation during active transcription
candidates.content: Abstract KAT5 is a prominent histone acetyltransferase that deposits acetylation on histone H4 to regulate transcription, genome stability, and cell fate decisions. Although the chromatin recruitment of KAT5 and its associated NuA4/TIP60 complex is well characterized, the molecular mechanisms that regulate its catalytic activity are still largely unknown. Here, we identify RNA as a direct and reversible modulator of KAT5 activity. Using single-end enhanced crosslinking and immunoprecipitation sequencing (seCLIP-seq), we find that KAT5 binds RNA in cells with a strong preference for GC-rich mRNA sequences enriched near transcription start sites. Unexpectedly, loss of KAT5–RNA interactions during acute transcriptional inhibition triggers rapid and pronounced promoter hyperacetylation. Biochemical and structural analyses suggest that RNA engages an RNA-sensing autoinhibitory region within the HAT domain, sterically blocking substrate access to the catalytic pocket and thereby suppressing KAT5 acetyltransferase activity. candidates.title: Nicking Loop™: streamlined circular DNA libraries for precise targeted sequencing and universal NGS read-out
candidates.content: Abstract Circular single-stranded DNA (CssDNA) offers unique advantages for molecular diagnostics and next-generation sequencing (NGS) due to its nuclease degradation resistance and compatibility with rolling circle amplification. CssDNA is used with several modern NGS platforms, but many library preparation workflows require a conversion step involving splinting and an enzymatic treatment, adding workflow complexity. This study introduces Nicking Loop™, a targeted library preparation method that converts single- and double-stranded DNA into CssDNA, enabling direct circular sequencing and controlled linear amplification that can be repeated over multiple generations. The method demonstrated improved preservation of variant allele frequencies across three amplification generations compared to PCR, which is particularly relevant for detection of low-abundance variants. candidates.title: Vintage Mistakes
candidates.content: This Nature article dives into a topic that’s always been divisive and is becoming more so all the time: what happens when a paper gets retracted? Does its full text still stay up on the journal website and other archives? Is it still searchable (and still fodder for AI/ML mining)? Can it still be cited? OK, now let’s go a step further. What if that paper has been in the literature for years when it turns out to be invalid? You have all those questions, and you can add some more: what about the citations that it has accumulated? The times it has been mentioned in review articles? Or how such publications and their faked data and conclusions can resurface using modern database searches? As many will have had cause to appreciate, just getting current bullshit retracted is already hard enough - now imagine trying to so something about it when everyone involved is dead. The article mentions the specific example of Vishwa Jit Gupta, who published hundreds of fraudulent papers about Himalayan fossils and geology in the 1960s, 70s, and 80s.
